title: Nanohertz Pendulum toward Macroscopic Entanglement under Structural Damping
authors: Azusa Sawada, Hina Nakano, Kanta Watanabe, Gaku Ohashi, Shota Okumura, Nobuyuki Matsumoto
abstract: Pendulums are attractive for macroscopic quantum control because gravity dilution reduces mechanical loss, while the $1/f$ force-noise spectrum associated with structural damping allows nearly lossless trapping to suppress the thermal noise sampled at an upward-shifted resonance. The same $1/f$ spectrum, however, produces a low-frequency tail that penalizes entanglement. With $10\%$ detection loss, we find that this tail raises the required back-action-to-thermal force-noise ratio by about $50\%$, corresponding to a required suspension gain $G_{\rm req}=1.49$. To overcome this structural-noise penalty, we realize a $7$-mg pendulum suspended by a stepped fused-silica fiber, with an energy-decay rate $Γ/2π=361(39)$ nHz ($Q\equivω_0/Γ=7.3(8)\times10^6$) at $ω_0/2π=2.63$ Hz. The reduction in $ω_0Γ$ yields a measured gain $G_q\simeq2.5$ relative to the previous monolithic device, exceeding the requirement.
summary: The research addresses the challenge of structural damping degrading quantum entanglement in macroscopic pendulums. By developing a theoretical model quantifying this penalty, the authors designed and experimentally implemented a novel stepped fused-silica suspension. This device achieved a measured mechanical gain significantly exceeding the required threshold, advancing the feasibility of high-fidelity quantum measurements at room temperature.
main_problem: The primary challenge is quantifying and mitigating the entanglement penalty imposed by the low-frequency tail (colored noise) originating from structural damping on macroscopic quantum entanglement measurements.
main_result: The authors successfully realized a 7-mg pendulum with a measured suspension gain ($G_q \simeq 2.5$) that significantly exceeds the theoretical requirement ($G_{	ext{req}} = 1.49$) needed to maintain measurable entanglement in the presence of structural noise.
method: The work combines advanced quantum modeling using closed-loop state-space dynamics (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck baths) with high-precision experimental measurements of mechanical dissipation via ring-down analysis on a custom stepped fiber suspension.
model_or_system: The physical system is a macroscopic pendulum suspended by a stepped fused-silica fiber, used in a continuous measurement setup. The theoretical model incorporates the full dynamics of the coupled cavity and mechanical modes, including structural damping modeled via auxiliary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck states.
key_observables: Logarithmic negativity ($	ext{EN}$), required suspension gain ($G_{	ext{req}}$), measured energy decay rate ($\Gamma/2\pi = 361(39)$ nHz), and the achieved mechanical suspension gain ($G_q \simeq 2.5$).
important_parameters: Detection loss ($\eta=0.9$), required structural-noise penalty factor (leading to $G_{	ext{req}}=1.49$), and the pendulum quality factor ($Q = 7.3(8) 	imes 10^6$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the structural bath using auxiliary Ornstein-Uhlenbeck states, and a key limitation noted is that residual loss from the upper attachment weld significantly lowers the achievable quality factor compared to ideal material limits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the excess low-frequency force noise tail due to structural damping (Fig. 1a), quantify the required gain versus detection efficiency (Fig. 1b), and show schematics/measurements of the stepped fiber suspension used for dissipation characterization (Fig. 1c).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from theoretical modeling of entanglement degradation due to colored noise in a closed-loop system, deriving a quantitative requirement ($G_{	ext{req}}$), to presenting the experimental realization using a novel stepped fiber suspension, and finally comparing the measured performance gain ($G_q$) against this derived threshold.
why_interesting: This work represents a crucial intersection of quantum sensing and mechanical engineering, demonstrating how advanced structural design (stepped fibers) can overcome fundamental noise limitations imposed by material damping to push macroscopic quantum measurements toward higher entanglement regimes.
